title: COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy: Analysing Twitter to Identify Barriers to Vaccination in a Low Uptake Region of the UK
screen_reason: Case study of 91,473 geo-located London COVID-19-vaccine tweets (30 November 2020 - 15 August 2021). An NLP platform ('Wordnerds') classified sentiment and clustered topics; the 8,189 negative-sentiment tweets (9 %) were clustered and 913 tweets from the top 12 negative clusters were manually coded by two researchers, who additionally tagged tweets 'posting false content (i.e., misinformation)'. 83 of those 913 tweets were tagged as misinformation ('just under 10% of the initial sample'), a share of platform items judged for veracity with a stated denominator = CONTENT. The estimate is heavily selection-biased (negative-sentiment, top-cluster subsample only) and the misinformation criterion is unusually lenient ('had not been verified from reputable sources'), so the row is flagged borderline with detailed caveats rather than dropped.

estimates.measure_type: % of the qualitatively analysed sample of negative-sentiment London COVID-19-vaccine tweets that were tagged as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 83 tweets (just under 10% of the initial sample) were identified as tweets that contained misinformation; sample = 913 tweets (83/913 = 9.1 %)
estimates.denominator: 913 tweets drawn by the NLP platform from the 12 most common negative-sentiment topic clusters (~1 % of the 91,473 tweets captured, and 11 % of the 8,189 tweets classified negative)
estimates.definition: tweet manually tagged by the researchers as posting false content (misinformation); the operational test was that the content it shared 'had not been verified from reputable sources'
estimates.misinfo_def: Whilst mapping tweets to one of our six vaccine hesitancy themes, tweets deemed to be posting false content (i.e., misinformation) about vaccines were also tagged by the researchers. A tweet was coded and tagged as misinformation if the content it shared had not been verified from reputable sources.
estimates.source_quote: More tweets were coded to the safety and then mistrust themes than any other; with 88 (29%) and 72 (23%) coded, respectively. Under-representation was the least mapped theme accounting for only 10 (3%) of coded tweets. 83 tweets (just under 10% of the initial sample) were identified as tweets that contained misinformation (see Figure 3).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Coding Tweets to Hesitancy Themes' (p. 4); Figure 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two researchers (KL, RG) independently coded the 913-tweet sample to six pre-set hesitancy themes and additionally tagged tweets as misinformation where the shared content 'had not been verified from reputable sources'; a third senior researcher (CM) sense-checked and all authors agreed a consolidated set. No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported, no named fact-checking source or claim list is used, and the upstream sentiment/topic selection was done by a commercial off-the-shelf NLP platform whose accuracy the authors themselves question (they note it mis-framed vaccine-passport tweets as vaccine barriers).
estimates.moderator_quote: The search strategy identified 91,473 initially relevant tweets. Of these, 82,284 were excluded due to the NLP tool classifying these tweets as having either positive or neutral underlying sentiment. The remaining 8,189 (9%) classified as having negative sentiment were fed through the NLP tool's topic analysis algorithm, which generated 12 clustered topics of discussion based on 913 of those tweets. The tweets contained within these 12 clusters represented ~1% of the tweets scraped in the initial search strategy and 11% of those classified as having negative sentiment.
estimates.notes: TWO JUDGEMENT CALLS an adjudicator must see. (a) DENOMINATOR: 9.1 % is a share of a doubly filtered subsample - only NEGATIVE-sentiment tweets, and only those the platform placed in the top 12 negative clusters (913 tweets, ~1 % of the 91,473 captured). It is therefore an upper-bound estimate within the most negative slice of the vaccine conversation, NOT the prevalence of misinformation among London vaccine tweets; the paper itself calls it 'the high proportion of tweets in our sample coded as misinformation'. If pooled with platform-wide content estimates it will bias the pooled value upward. A whole-corpus figure is not derivable: 83/91,473 would be a severe undercount because only 913 tweets were ever screened for misinformation, so it is not computed (R8). (b) CONSTRUCT VALIDITY / breadth: the coding rule tags a tweet whose content 'had not been verified from reputable sources', so an unverified but true claim could be labelled misinformation. That is why breadth is coded as the loosest category (misleading) and borderline=true. Because the tag is nonetheless explicitly for 'posting false content (i.e., misinformation)', I kept construct=CONTENT rather than QUALITY, but an adjudicator may reasonably reclassify. Value: 83 and 913 are both verbatim counts with the same denominator, so 9.1 % is permitted under R8; the paper's own wording 'just under 10%' is looser. Year coded 2020 (window opens 30 Nov 2020) although most of the collection period falls in 2021.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The hesitancy-theme shares (safety 88 = 29 %, mistrust 72 = 23 %, under-representation 10 = 3 %, of the 302 tweets codable to a theme) are attitude/barrier codings, not misinformation numerators, so no rows. (2) The 9 % of the 91,473 tweets classified as NEGATIVE sentiment (8,189 tweets) is a sentiment share, not misinformation - deliberately not extracted, even though 9 % coincidentally resembles the misinformation share within the sample. (3) 302/913 (33.1 %) tweets 'provided enough detail to contextualise the negative sentiment' - a codability rate, not prevalence. (4) Figure 3 ('Chart to quantify the results of the coding exercise') presumably cross-tabulates misinformation by theme, but the figure content is not in the text extraction, so any theme-level misinformation shares are unavailable. (5) The paper states misinformation tweets were 'heavily biased towards safety, mistrust, and efficacy concerns' and that a small minority of inaccurate tweets were pro-vaccination, with no counts - within-misinformation composition only. (6) No exposure, reach, engagement or concentration measure is reported (no retweet/impression data), so there is no EXPOSURE or CONCENTRATION row. (7) Data are geo-located London Twitter accounts only; the authors flag that London Twitter users are not demographically representative of Londoners.

rob.design: Cross-sectional 'soft-intelligence' case study. Frame: prospective collection via Twitter advanced search of geo-located London tweets matching a COVID-19-vaccine keyword string, 30 November 2020 - 15 August 2021; 91,473 tweets captured. Selection: a commercial NLP platform (Wordnerds) assigned sentiment, excluding 82,284 positive/neutral tweets, then clustered the 8,189 negative tweets and produced a 913-tweet sample from the top 12 negative clusters (~1 % of the corpus). Coding: two researchers independently mapped the 913 tweets to six a priori hesitancy themes (derived from the WHO SAGE 3C model) and tagged misinformation where content was unverified by reputable sources; a third senior researcher sense-checked; consensus reached by all authors. Reliability: NO kappa or agreement statistic reported. Key weaknesses acknowledged by the authors: platform mis-classification of context (vaccine passports), exclusion of neutral-sentiment tweets that may carry hesitancy, incomplete search vocabulary (e.g. 'jab' omitted), non-representative Twitter demographics, and no demographic data (anonymised). Self-described as a small feasibility case study rather than a prevalence study.
